# Research brief: `javax.crypto.Cipher`, CipherSpec finding "no generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed"

**Source limits**
- My tools returned only search-result excerpts, not full documents. I could not open the raw `Cipher.crysl` file directly. The rule text below comes from an excerpt of the GitHub view of the same file: https://github.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/blob/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl
- That excerpt skips lines. I saw `i1`–`i4`, one `CONSTRAINTS` block, and the `generatedKey` line. I did not see the full `EVENTS`, `ORDER`, `REQUIRES` or `ENSURES` sections.
- I did not verify the SHA-256 (`da73b53a…`) against the file.
- Some statements below are my inference from the CrySL documentation, not text in the rule file. I mark these.

## Q1. What `Cipher` governs, and what the finding refers to

**What `Cipher` governs**
- The Java 8 Javadoc says Cipher "forms the core of the Java Cryptographic Extension (JCE) framework". It provides encryption and decryption. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- An application creates a Cipher by calling `getInstance` with a transformation name.
- A transformation is either `algorithm` or `algorithm/mode/padding`. In the short form, provider-specific defaults apply for mode and padding. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- `init(int opmode, Key key[, …])` and `init(int opmode, Certificate …)` initialize the cipher. The Cipher docs say initializing a Cipher resets it as if it were a new instance. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html

**What the finding refers to**
- The finding concerns the `key` argument of an `init(encmode, key …)` event.
- In the rule's `OBJECTS` block, `key` is declared as `java.security.Key`. The `CONSTRAINTS` block contains this clause:
  > `generatedKey[key, alg(transformation)] || generatedPubkey[key] || generatedPrivkey[key];`
- This is a CrySL predicate. It states that the key object must carry one of these labels. It is not a Java API value or event.
- The label comes from another class's rule. CrySL "REQUIRES" blocks demand a predicate that another rule "ENSURES". https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/
- The CrySL documentation and papers give these producers of `generatedKey`:
  - The `KeyGenerator` rule ensures `generatedKey[key, algorithm]` (ECOOP 2018 paper: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol109-ecoop2018/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10.pdf).
  - The `SecretKeySpec` rule requires `randomized[keyMaterial]` and ensures `generatedKey[this, alg]` (https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/).
  - The `SecretKeyFactory` rule ensures `generatedKey[this, cipherAlg]`, after `PBEKeySpec` produces `speccedKey` (https://www.bodden.de/pubs/krueger20cognicryptgen.pdf).
- So "no generator observed" means the analysis found no tracked producer of such a predicate for the key object.
- Unresolved: the exact internal meaning of the detector's message. The detector version and its message-to-error mapping were not supplied.

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and recommended remediation

**What the official docs say**
- Cipher Javadoc (Java 25) API note: use a transformation that fully specifies algorithm, mode and padding. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- The JDK Providers document says defaults are provider-specific and can vary among providers. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/10/security/oracle-providers.htm
- If a cipher needs parameters that can't be derived from the key, the implementation generates them for encryption or wrapping. Decryption or unwrapping fails instead. The values can be read back with `getParameters` or `getIV`. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- The Java 8 Javadoc says that if params is null, the implementation generates required parameters for encryption and raises `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException` for decryption. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- GCM has a uniqueness requirement on IVs for a given key. Repeated IVs allow forgery. Callers should re-initialize the cipher with GCM parameters that have a different IV after each encryption. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 have a similar unique-nonce requirement. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- The JCA Reference Guide's GCM example uses `Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")` with `init(mode, key, params)`. For decryption, the same AAD and GCM parameters must be supplied. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- `GCMParameterSpec` carries the IV and the tag bit-length. https://download.java.net/java/early_access/jdk27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec.html

**Key provenance**
- `KeyGenerator` generates secret keys. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html
- `SecretKeySpec` builds a key from caller-supplied bytes. It does not generate randomness. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html
- I found no official Oracle text that names a "generated key" requirement or prescribes remediation for this finding. That requirement comes from the CrySL rule, which is a policy choice by CROSSING/CogniCrypt, not the JCA contract.
- The CrySL docs' implied remedy is to obtain the key from a producer the rule model recognises. Examples are `KeyGenerator`, `SecretKeyFactory` via `PBEKeySpec`, or `SecretKeySpec` over randomized bytes. https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/

## Q3. Compatibility when usage changes

**What the docs support**
- Decryption must reuse the same transformation, key and IV or parameters. The JCA guide's AES example notes the same IV is needed for encryption and decryption. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- For AEAD modes such as GCM, the authentication tag is appended on encryption and verified on decryption. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html
- Changing only where the key comes from does not change the Cipher API contract. I found no source that says it changes the persisted or wire format.
- Changing the transformation, mode, padding, tag length or IV handling does change the format. Existing ciphertext is then not readable without the old parameters. I did not find an official statement of this beyond the points above.
- Changing a short transformation such as `"AES"` to a fully specified one is supported by the docs' recommendation above. Existing data written under a provider default is compatible only if the explicit transformation matches that default. The JDK SunJCE defaults were not extracted from the sources I saw.

**Platform support**
- The Javadoc cannot be treated as a complete platform matrix. Java 8 documents `Cipher` as "Since: 1.5".
- Java 8 lists required transformations: AES/CBC and ECB variants, plus DES and others. The excerpt did not show AES/GCM in that list. I did not confirm it.
- Java 17's Javadoc says implementations must support the listed transformations and refers to the Standard Algorithm Names spec. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- The SunJCE table (JDK 10 Providers doc) lists AES with GCM/NoPadding. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/10/security/oracle-providers.htm
- Unresolved: the exact first JDK version with AES/GCM in SunJCE. I did not confirm it.
- Unresolved: provider and jurisdiction key-size limits. The SunJCE docs list restrictions for AES key sizes. Third-party providers may differ.

**Migration**
- I found no official migration guide for this finding. Oracle documentation gives general guidance only.

## Q4. What the CrySL rule itself states

**Receiver and method names**
- The rule begins `SPEC javax.crypto.Cipher`. The CrySL docs say the SPEC clause names "the fully qualified class name the following specification holds for". https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/
- Visible `init` events in the excerpt:
  - `i1: init(encmode, certificate);`
